uncited: Per-tile sorting and per-pixel resorting is a rasterization strategy designed to mitigate "popping" artifacts in surface-based volumetric representations (such as 2DGS and QGS) where Gaussian distributions are concentrated on surfaces.

It addresses the sensitivity of alpha-blending order by replacing inconsistent per-ray depth sorting with a two-stage approach: coarse global ordering via per-tile depth approximation and fine local ordering via per-pixel resorting.

This method sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing strict consistency between forward rendering and backward gradient computation traversal orders, thereby eliminating streak-like and blocky artifacts introduced by single-ray approximations.
The method operates on a tile-based rasterization pipeline, building on [Tile-based Depth Sorting](8038-tile-based-depth-sorting.md).
It assumes a tile size of $16 \times 16$ pixels, resulting in 256 pixels per tile.
*   Camera parameters (origin $\hat{\mathbf{o}}$, ray direction $\hat{\mathbf{r}}$).
*   Set of projected 3D Gaussians (or quadric primitives) covering the current tile.
*   Gaussian properties: opacity $\alpha$, scale, rotation, color, normal, curvature, etc.
*   Final rendered color, depth, normal, and other volumetric maps $\hat{X}$ for each pixel.
**Tile Depth Buffer:** A single depth value $d_{tile}$ per $16 \times 16$ tile.
**Gaussian Property Buffer:** An array of size 8 used to store intermediate Gaussian properties (depth, normal, etc.) for a specific pixel before blending.
This buffer acts as a local priority queue or staging area.
**Sorted Gaussian List:** A list of Gaussians covering the tile, sorted by the tile depth $d_{tile}$.
For each $16 \times 16$ pixel tile, identify the pixel closest to the projected vertex of the underlying quadric surface (or the centroid of the Gaussians).
Compute the intersection depth $d_{tile}$ along the ray from this specific pixel.
Apply this single depth value $d_{tile}$ to all 256 pixels in the tile.
Use $d_{tile}$ to perform global sorting of all Gaussians covering the tile.
This removes streak-like inconsistencies but may introduce blocky artifacts due to the single-ray approximation.
*   Retrieve the globally sorted list of Gaussians.
*   Filter and reorder the Gaussians based on the actual per-ray depth for that specific pixel.
This step eliminates the blocky artifacts introduced in Step 1.
*   Store the calculated properties (depth, normal, opacity $\alpha$, etc.) of the Gaussians in the 8-length buffer array.
*   Once the buffer is full (or when processing the final Gaussian), select the closest Gaussian (front-most) for alpha-blending.
This ensures a strict near-to-far traversal order.
Perform alpha-blending in the near-to-far order established by the resorting.
*   $N$ is the number of Gaussians along the ray.
*   $\bar{\alpha}_i = \alpha_i g_i$ is the effective opacity (product of Gaussian opacity $\alpha_i$ and visibility factor $g_i$).
*   $T_i = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \bar{\alpha}_j)$ is the accumulated transmittance before Gaussian $i$.
*   $X_i$ represents the property value of the $i$-th Gaussian.
Compute gradients in the same near-to-far order as the forward pass to ensure consistency.
This front-to-back form ensures the backward computation follows the same order as the forward computation.
Note that the distortion loss gradient does not require modification as its computation order is unaffected.
This likely refers to a hardware register or cache line constraint for local sorting, ensuring that the closest 8 Gaussians are readily accessible for blending.
Degenerate cases where the ray is parallel to the surface or the intersection is undefined should be handled by falling back to a default depth or skipping the Gaussian.
If the backward pass uses a different order (e.g., far-to-near) than the forward pass (near-to-far), the gradients will be incorrect, leading to training instability.
The rewritten gradient formula ensures alignment.
*   **Time Complexity:** The global sort is $O(N \log N)$ or $O(N)$ with radix sort, where $N$ is the number of Gaussians per tile.

The per-pixel resorting adds a local sorting cost, effectively making the total complexity $O(P \cdot K \log K)$, where $P$ is the number of pixels in the tile (256) and $K$ is the number of Gaussians per pixel.
This is generally more expensive than simple per-ray sorting but reduces popping artifacts.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires storage for the tile depth buffer and the per-pixel property buffer.
